sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We have only a few weeks of Amsterdam data with comparable history, so there is no trend yet; the figures are for weekdays in August and September 2026.

Amsterdam has gone furthest in making the car expensive rather than forbidden. In 2019 the street in the old centre went to €7.50 an hour [0], and the city set out to remove roughly 7,000 to 10,000 street spaces over seven years, partly by moving parking into garages [1]. Permits have risen repeatedly and paid hours now run to midnight in many neighbourhoods [2], and the 2026 coalition agreement promises dearer permits and smaller visitor discounts [6]. The zero-emission zones target vans, taxis and freight; private cars face only a diesel restriction [5]. The city has also been shrinking park-and-ride, closing P+R Zeeburg 1 in 2025 [4]. Day visits remain below 2019 (21.9 million against 24.1 million) [12].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
Since February 2024 the municipal garages charge the same as the street around them, so a garage is no longer a cheaper way to park in the centre; Albert Cuyp, for example, went from €5.10 to €6.50 an hour [3]. The next move may be fewer central garages: the coalition wants to talk about closing the Bijenkorf garage on the Damrak, run by Q-Park, for housing [7].

Amsterdam leads the Netherlands on charging, with about 16,000 points [8]. It also publishes live availability for its garages and P+R sites as open data [9], and operators sell reservations and plate-based entry, as at Q-Park's Centraal garage [10].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Two operators hold almost all the capacity: Q-Park (about 36 garages, 15,000 spaces) and the municipality (about 31 sites, 14,500 spaces, including the big P+R garages at the ArenA). Interparking, the Oosterdok garage and a large number of small private spaces sold through apps such as ParkBee make up the rest.

Prices fall steeply with distance from the Dam, from €9 an hour and €65 a day within a kilometre to under €4 and €35 beyond two. Occupancy runs the other way: about a third of spaces are used near the Dam, 43% further out. Municipal garages, cheaper than Q-Park (typically €3.70 against €4.80 an hour), are fuller on weekdays (49% against 27%). The extremes are telling. The municipal Albert Cuyp garage is 90% full at €6.96, while Interparking's Rembrandtplein, at €13 an hour, is 10% full. At these prices a central garage is a premium product, used by those who must park there.
